chapter_theme: The second ten, Kumattur Kannanar's songs for Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan: the felling of the enemy's guardian kadamba at sea told as Murugan's killing of Sur, the drum made from that tree, enemy lands ruined against the guarded land that flowers, the queen left waiting while the king stays in camp, and a giver who will not fail even when the rains do; the preface adds his parents, the Himalayan bow and the binding of the Yavanas.

11.reading: The poet tells Cheralathan, whose army kills in war and who drinks strained toddy, that just as Murugan, reaching the great sea, cut down Sur at the root and rode his elephant, the king went to the sea, turned the dark backwater red with the blood of the foes his spears tore open, and felled at the root the guarded kadamba that many had tended, and so the poet delights to see his much-praised wealth as he rides his tusker with its gold-ornamented neck, the king who broke the valour of every ruler from the Himalaya of the Aryans to Kumari in the south.
11.nuance: Line 5 (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த) and line 13 (கடியுடை முழுமுதல் துமிய) are built on the same words, so the felling of the enemy's guardian kadamba is told as a repetition of the god's killing of Sur; the simile is the frame of the deed, not decoration. The red backwater like vermilion paste (line 10) is the only colour in the battle; the closing lines reach from the Himalaya to Kumari, the usual measure of a Tamil king's claim.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's wealth and victory as he sees it

comparisons.tenor: the king who felled the enemy's kadamba at sea and rides his elephant
the dark backwater reddened by the blood of the wounded

12.reading: The poet tells the king who cut the kadamba at its root, making rival kings tremble, that as the herds of other beasts quake when the maned lion walks the slope, so kings in their drum-loud towns cannot sleep for his fame, which is sweet to hear; and that his feasting is sweet to share, for the poet's large hungry kin, brought over many hills where a young elephant fans off bees beside its mother, have eaten fat meat cut with the knife, white rice with mutton and clear toddy until their old hunger ended, put off rags like a wet kite's wing, wrapped on fine cloth, and seen their women adorned with jewels.
12.nuance: The poem is built on two parallel predicates, கேட்டற்கு இனிது (line 9: sweet to hear) and நுகர்தற்கு இனிது (line 25: sweet to enjoy): the king's fame is a terror for kings and a feast for bards, and the same wealth is meant by both. தொல்பசி (line 15), an old, inherited hunger, makes the gift the end of a condition, not a meal.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's fame and of the feast he gave the bard's kin

comparisons.vehicle: அரிமான் வழங்கும் சாரல் பிறமான் தோடுகொள் இனநிரை
comparisons.tenor: rival kings who cannot sleep for the king's fame

13.reading: The poet contrasts the lands the king entered in anger, once rich watered country where bulls sowed unploughed fields, buffaloes waded among sugarcane and neythal, and old cows grazed on water-lilies by the dancing grounds, now a waste like a body Death has seized, where a ghoul-woman rides a demon over thorny scrub and the dust of empty commons, with his own guarded land, where forests are for the gods, pastures for warriors and their women, families are protected, Venus keeps its course, rain falls where it is wanted, and disease and hunger have left, so that the land flowers.
13.nuance: The poem sets the same kind of country twice, destroyed and flourishing, and the hinge is the king's anger (நீ சிவந்து இறுத்த, line 12) against his guarding (நீ காத்த, line 28). Lines 25 and 26 take the sky as witness: Venus not straying and rain coming on demand are signs of good rule, not luck.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king through the fate of the lands he ruins and the land he guards

comparisons.tenor: the rich land laid waste by the king's invasion

14.reading: The poet tells the king that he is as beyond measure as earth, water, wind and sky, as bright as the stars, planets, moon, sun and fire joined in one light, as open-handed as Akkuran who fought beside the hundred, unshakable even if Death came in anger, the shield of the worthy, husband of a queen whose beauty rivals the celestial women, ploughman whose plough is his army, king of the singing woman, and wishes that like the first kings of his line who ruled the whole sea-bounded earth he may stand with undying fame as long as this world.
14.nuance: The opening counts the elements as four, not five, and gives the light its own list of five (stars, planets, moon, sun, fire); the king is matched to the sky's sum, not to one body in it. படைஏர் உழவ (line 17) turns the army into a plough, the war king pictured as a farmer. The poem says nothing of Akkuran beyond his fight among the hundred.

thinai_evidence.note: a catalogue of the king's qualities ending in a blessing

comparisons.vehicle: நாள்கோள் திங்கள் ஞாயிறு கனைஅழல் ஐந்(து)ஒருங்கு புணர்ந்த விளக்கத்(து)

comparisons.tenor: the king who works his army as a ploughman works his plough
the king's lasting rule and fame

15.reading: The poet tells Cheralathan that he has seen the lands of the enemies who forgot his might and opposed him, where his army camped year after year, burned the outposts, broke the walls' trees and turned the old towns to waste, so that white-flowered velai, gourd and peer creepers spread over the dry tank-beds and old houses and only base men with stinking bows walk there; and that he has also seen with wonder the king's own good land of sea, hill and river, with its unfailing festivals, its drums, its blessing bards and the worthy who keep from hell and live free of distress under his care, and so he has come, loving his many qualities and his fame like Nediyon's.
15.nuance: The poem is told as two sights, கண்டுவந் திசினே (line 15) and கண்டுமதி மருண்டனென் (line 34): the poet's eye witnesses both the ruin and the plenty, so the praise rests on what he saw, not on report. The guarded land is defined by its people (bards who bless the world, the worthy who shun hell) as much as by its riches.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet reports what he saw of the ruined and the guarded lands to praise the king

16.reading: Because the king has lingered long in his war camp, where young elephants with tusks blunted from breaking the tall gates of fortress walls hung with the ayyavi roar in musth, the poet has come to see him, and asks whether the bed of his queen, of settled chastity and gentle grace, who speaks sweetly even when she sulks and has every right to think of him, will escape its loneliness, since his soft chest, bright with gems, gold and diamonds and the garland of seven crowns, which could be the bed where her eyes sleep, now torments her.
16.nuance: A puram poem that turns at line 10 to the queen's waiting: the same jewelled chest that wears the seven crowns' garland (line 17, as in 14 line 11) is her pillow and the cause of her pain. பூணா ஐயவி (line 4) separates the ayyavi of the siege from the white mustard a new mother wears, a pun on one word. Lines 14 and 18 to 19 are hard to construe, so the reading of the queen's lines is tentative.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet comes to the war camp to see and praise the king

17.reading: The poet tells the king of the green ornament, king of the singing woman, that nothing can be found to match him, since he accepts the tribute of foes who bow even when they are at fault; his great victorious drum, made from the kadamba he cut down after driving back the sea, is beaten by armleted drummers after offerings are scattered, and his sky-touching white umbrella, under rain-clouds and wheeling winds, proclaims to the wide world that has found no other refuge: come to this shade.
17.nuance: The drum is made of the enemy's felled guardian tree, so every beating of it repeats the victory of 11 and 12. The umbrella's call, வருக இந் நிழல் (line 9), makes the king's protection an open invitation rather than a conquest.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king as without equal, by his drum and umbrella

18.reading: Drink the toddy, cook the rice, cut the meat, set the stew on the fire, give to all who come without limit while the gold vessels clink, let the dancing women with dark curling hair serve from the hearths, and share what you have received without fault, the poet tells the bards, for even if the cloud that has taken on the care of the earth fails for many years and the rain lies, Cheralathan will not betray their hope.
18.nuance: The commands are to the bards, not the king: the gift is to be passed on at once (பெற்றது உதவுமின், line 7), so the king's giving becomes the bards' hospitality. The rain is not a model he equals but one he outdoes, since rain can fail.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's unfailing giving

comparisons.tenor: Cheralathan's giving, which does not fail

19.reading: The poet tells the king that, with his plundering goblin-like scouts cutting through the stony road, his warriors drawing spears from tiger-skin sheaths, and his drummers beating the war drum after an offering of red millet mixed with blood, he so loves the work of war with his companions who never take off their armour that he grants no grace even to his modest, bright-browed wife, who lives with him only in dreams on the rare night he sleeps; and that the lands he ravaged, where he forbade the plough and the people fled, once had lotus and water-lily in every pond, neythal in the paddy, reapers' sickles bending and sugar presses groaning, so that onlookers clap their hands in pity, saying these were good only yesterday, and many fine lands have come to nothing.
19.nuance: The colophon calls this a song of the gift (பரிசிற்றுறை), but the poem asks for nothing: it sets the king's love of war against two losses, his wife's and the ravaged farmers'. The onlookers' words (lines 24 and 25) are the poem's only voice of grief. The syntax of lines 9 to 15 (who is pitied, and by whom) is hard, and the reading of the wife's lines is tentative.

thinai_evidence.note: the army's march, the war-drum rite and the ravaging of enemy farmland

20.reading: If you ask who our king is, says the poet, he is Neduncheralathan, who went against his foes on an island in the sea and cut down the kadamba at its root: may his garland live; his deeds against enemies never failed by a mote of sunlit dust, he is false neither in enemy land nor even in dreams, he crushed the proud and stormed moated, walled forts, he scatters horses, elephants and chariots to drummers and players without stint, and with a heart that does not swerve in the duty of giving, to our people or others, skilled or unskilled, he will not let a belly go hungry even if the rains fail for many years: may the womb of the mother who bore him be free of blemish.
20.nuance: The poem is shaped as an answer to a stranger's question (நும்கோ யார், line 1), the form a bard uses to send another to his patron. The blessing falls not on the king but on his mother's womb (line 27), so the praise ends by honouring where he came from. Truthfulness is claimed even in dreams (கனவினும், line 10).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's truthfulness and giving

comparisons.tenor: the king's giving, which does not fail

patikam:2.reading: The decade's preface says that Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan, son of Udhiyan Cheral of the sweet-sounding drum by Nallini of the Veliyan Vel line, carved his bow on the Himalaya, set up his rule so that the sea-fenced Tamil land shone, made the Aryans bow, bound the harsh-spoken Yavanas, poured ghee on their heads and tied their hands behind them, took their costly vessels and diamonds to his old city and gave to others, and that Kumattur Kannanar sang this ten.
patikam:2.nuance: The preface supplies what the songs leave out: the king's parents, the Himalayan bow and the humiliation of the Yavanas. The seized treasure is at once given away (பிறர்க்கு உதவி, line 11), the same pairing of conquest and gift as in 12 and 20.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's lineage, conquests and giving

comparisons.tenor: the sea that bounds the Tamil land

links.note: Patitruppattu 11 likens the Chera, who reached the sea and felled the enemy's guarded kadamba at the root (முழுமுதல் துமிய), to Murugan who cut down Sur at the root (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த); Thirumurugatruppadai 45-60 tells the god's deed itself: he entered the cold sea and cut Sur at the root (சூர்முதல் தடிந்த), the mango at its trunk.
links.teaches: Thirumurugatruppadai shows that cutting the root in the sea was already the god's signature deed, so the Chera poet's repeated phrase is a claim that the king's sea raid re-enacted Murugan's myth, with the enemy's guardian tree standing in for Sur's tree.

links.note: Kural 734 defines a land as one free of crushing hunger, unceasing disease and destructive foes; Patitruppattu 13 ends that the land the king guards has flowered, rid of disease and hunger (நோயொடு பசி இகந்து), after showing the enemy lands he ruined.
links.teaches: The Kural states the absences that make a land; the Chera poem shows who secures them and at whose cost, since the same king's anger is the destructive foe of his neighbours, so the definition is met at home by being broken next door.

links.note: Purananuru 117 says Pari's land kept its rain even when Venus ran to the south and other evil signs appeared; Patitruppattu 13 says that in the king's guarded land Venus does not run into the burning quarter and rain stands where it is wanted.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show two views of the omen: the lament makes a just ruler's land immune to the bad sign, while the Chera praise has the good ruler prevent the sign itself, so royal virtue was imagined as reaching even the planets' course.

links.note: Purananuru 2 likens Udhiyan Cheralathan's patience, counsel, strength, wrath and grace to the five great elements; Patitruppattu 14 tells his son, named in the decade's preface as Udhiyan Cheral's son, that he is as beyond measure as earth, water, wind and sky.
links.teaches: Father and son are both praised through the elements, which shows the element catalogue working as a Chera family formula, and the son's version moves the point from the elements' separate qualities to their shared immeasurability.

links.note: Purananuru 20 says that even if one could measure the sea's depth, the earth's breadth, the wind's paths and the sky, the Chera's knowledge, compassion and kindness could not be measured; Patitruppattu 14 says the king is as immeasurable as earth, water, wind and sky.
links.teaches: One poet makes the elements measurable so that the king can exceed them, the other makes them the standard of the unmeasurable, which shows that the same four-part catalogue could rank a king either above nature or alongside it.

links.note: Both are reports of having seen the enemy's ruined land (கண்டனென் in Purananuru 23, கண்டுவந் திசினே in Patitruppattu 15), and both mark the ruin by white velai flowers growing over it (வேளை வெண்பூ; வெண்பூ வேளை).
links.teaches: The shared white velai shows it was a stock sign of a razed settlement in both Pandya and Chera praise, and Patitruppattu 15 extends the form: where Purananuru 23 ends on the waste, the Chera poet adds a second sight, the king's own guarded land, so the ruin becomes one half of a judgment on rule.

links.note: The same line, எழுமுடி கெழீஇய திருஞெமர் அகலத்து, describes the king's chest in 14 line 11, where it is the shield of the worthy, and in 16 line 17, where it is the queen's longed-for bed.
links.teaches: The decade reuses one formula of the crowned chest for war and for love, so the turn in 16 to the waiting queen is built from the same praise language and makes the protector of the realm the cause of her loneliness.

links.note: 16 asks whether the queen's bed will escape loneliness while the king lingers in camp; 19 says his love of war leaves no grace even for his modest wife, who has him only in dreams on the rare night he sleeps.
links.teaches: Taken together, the two poems show the decade returning to the queen's cost of war as a counter-voice inside praise, and 19 sharpens the question of 16 into a charge, set beside the ruin of the enemy's farmers.

links.note: Patitruppattu 17 says the king's great victory drum was made from the kadamba he cut after driving back the sea (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய வலம்படு வியன்பணை); in Akananuru 347 the heroine compares the street's gossip to the drum of Cheralathan who drove back the sea and cut the kadamba (கடம்பு அறுத்து இயற்றிய பண்ணமை முரசின்).
links.teaches: The near-identical wording shows an akam poet borrowing the Chera's victory drum, a puram fact, to measure how loud gossip is, so the king's war trophy had become familiar enough to serve as a household simile for noise.

links.note: Kural 211 makes the rain the model of giving that seeks no return; Patitruppattu 18 says that even if the rain-cloud fails for many years, Cheralathan will not fail the bards' hope.
links.teaches: The Kural treats rain as the standard for duty-bound giving, but the Chera poem ranks the king above that standard because rain can fail, so the bards' praise claims for a patron a reliability the ethics book grants only to nature.

links.note: Both close on the failure of rain: 18 says Cheralathan will not lie even if rain fails for many years (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல துளக்கி ... தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையாது மாறி); 20 repeats the lines for the drought (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல மாறித் தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையா(து) ஆயினும்) and adds that he will not let a belly go hungry.
links.teaches: The repeated lines show that the decade has a fixed formula for drought, and 20 turns the general promise of 18 into a concrete guarantee against hunger, ending in a blessing on the mother who bore the giver.

links.note: The preface says the king carved his bow on the Himalaya and brought costly vessels with diamonds (அருவிலை நன்கலம் வயிரமொடு கொண்டு) to his old city and gave to others; Akananuru 127 recalls Cheralathan who drove off the sea, cut the kadamba, carved his bow on the Himalaya and heaped the foes' tribute of fine vessels with diamonds (நன்கலம் ... வயிரமொடு) at Maanthai, leaving it for the earth to eat.
links.teaches: The two record the same hoard with the same jewel list but different fates, given away in the preface and left buried in the akam poem, so an akam poet could cite a puram event precisely while turning its moral from royal giving to abandoned wealth, the wealth the lover will not linger for.

new_concepts.gloss: the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the text names it: பரிசிலர் வெறுக்கை (15 line 21), பரிசில் மாக்கள் (20 line 22), and the colophon of 19, பரிசிற்றுறைப் பாடாண்பாட்டு; the same id is already used in the Purananuru marks

source_issues: 11-20: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the thurais are paadaan forms, and all but 19 are marked paadaan here. The patikam has neither thinai nor thurai.
19: the colophon thurai is பரிசிற்றுறைப் பாடாண்பாட்டு, but the poem asks for no gift; it describes the march, the war-drum rite and ravaged farmland, so it is marked vanji here.
13 lines 1-2: words are run together without spaces (தொறுத்தவயல் ஆரல்பிறழ்நவும், ஏறுபொருதசெறு உழாதுவித்துநவும்); the division is the reader's.
16 line 17 repeats 14 line 11 (எழுமுடி கெழீஇய திருஞெமர் அகலத்து) apart from the sandhi ப்; the repeated_line flag lists 16 and 40 but misses 14.
18 lines 8-10 and 20 lines 24-25 share the drought formula (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல ... தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையா...), with துளக்கி / மாறித் varying; not flagged.
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags): 15 lines 33 and 37, 19 line 12, 20 line 22; the repaired readings are plausible.
patikam:2 line 14 (குமட்டூர்க் கண்ணனார் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line, as the ingest notes say.
20 line 10 has a comma inside the line (கனவினும், ஒன்னார்) where the sentence begun in line 9 ends; harmless.
